experience.description: Owned and delivered a facility-automation tool end to end for the HISinOne platform — architecture through live production and verification.

paragraphs: HFT Stuttgart's facility team needed to keep two separate platforms, WebUntis and HISinOne, in sync by hand — entering building and room data from spreadsheets into the system of record. It was slow and quietly error-prone: duplicated rooms, missed floors, records that drifted out of sync with reality, with no way to know how many mistakes existed until someone found one.

I owned the tool end to end. I built a SOAP/WSDL client against WebUntis (via Zeep) and an authenticated API client against HISinOne, then designed a hierarchical resolution pipeline that normalizes facility data through building → floor → room, resolving each level independently and flagging ambiguous matches instead of guessing. Automatic detection catches missing records before they reach production, and a pytest-driven automated test suite — 100% passing — runs against every change.

The tool processed 200+ records across 10+ buildings in its first live run with zero errors, and ran independent post-import verification to prove that, not just claim it. It's now how the team actually imports facility data, not a one-off script someone ran once.

experience.description: Rebuilt Letstream's real-time logistics dashboard in Angular and led the team's migration off Vue.

paragraphs: The logistics dashboard was built in Vue, but the rest of the team's stack had already moved to Angular — so it was both out of step with everything else and slow under real load, with sync lag and initial loads that made the tool frustrating to use during live tracking.

I rebuilt it as a reactive, role-based Angular application using RxJS streams, replacing broad data fetches with custom lazy-loading and GraphQL fragment optimization — cutting initial load time by 40% and improving real-time sync speed by 25%. I also reduced server overhead by 30% through debounce techniques and disciplined Angular lifecycle management (OnInit/OnDestroy), and led two developers through the Vue-to-Angular migration myself, establishing coding standards and mentoring practices that cut code-review cycle time by 15%.

I partnered closely with backend engineers on end-to-end testing across the platform, validating that data flowed correctly between frontend and backend services and catching integration issues before release — because a logistics dashboard that's wrong under load is worse than one that's just slow.

experience.description: Built Eber end to end — the Angular frontend and the Node.js/Express/MongoDB backend — for a full-stack, on-demand ride-booking platform.

paragraphs: Elluminati Ventures needed a ride-booking platform that handled the full lifecycle of a ride — request, match, track, pay, complete — not a UI mockup of one, built across the whole stack by one person.
I built the Angular 18 frontend: real-time Google Maps tracking, live ride updates over WebSockets, and Stripe payment processing, inside a responsive, PWA-enabled interface.

On the backend, I built the Node.js/Express/MongoDB service powering the full ride lifecycle — from driver assignment through trip completion, dynamic pricing and automated invoice generation — and the REST APIs for that lifecycle, tested in Postman and designed to be consumed by both the admin panel and future mobile clients.

I implemented multi-channel notifications (Twilio SMS, Nodemailer email, browser push) to keep riders and drivers updated at every stage of a trip, and built an admin dashboard with ride history, filtering, CSV export and live trip-path visualization using Google Maps polylines.

engineeringPrinciples.label: Features
engineeringPrinciples.statement: Start with the problem, not the feature.
engineeringPrinciples.explanation: I translate a stated problem into the smallest system that actually solves it — a facility team needed accurate records, not a dashboard; a logistics team needed faster sync, not a rewrite for its own sake.

engineeringPrinciples.label: Systems
engineeringPrinciples.statement: Build the simplest system that remains understandable as it grows.
engineeringPrinciples.explanation: I prefer systems whose boundaries, responsibilities and trade-offs remain understandable as the product evolves.

engineeringPrinciples.label: Trade-offs
engineeringPrinciples.statement: Every engineering decision moves complexity somewhere.
engineeringPrinciples.explanation: Every case study I write documents the alternative I didn't choose and why — a decision is only honest once its cost is named, not just its benefit.

engineeringPrinciples.label: Reliability
engineeringPrinciples.statement: A system is only as reliable as the behavior you can verify.
engineeringPrinciples.explanation: I treat verification as part of the deliverable — automated tests, independent checks and explicit failure handling, not code that happened to work once.

services.title: Full-stack Development
services.description: TypeScript applications from interface to API and database, shipped with automated tests and CI/CD.

paragraphs: I don't treat "full-stack" as switching hats between frontend and backend — it's owning the whole path a piece of data takes, from a database schema through an API contract to the component that renders it, so nothing gets lost in translation at the boundaries.

That's shown up directly in projects like SynthGraph's lineage pipeline and Eber's ride-booking platform, where I designed the schema, built the API and shipped the UI that consumes it, with automated tests and CI/CD gating every change before it reaches production.

services.title: Frontend Engineering
services.description: Reactive Angular and React interfaces with real-time data and attention to load performance.

paragraphs: Real-time data is the part that actually breaks frontend code — a UI that looks right in a demo can fall apart under live updates, race conditions and slow networks. I build interfaces that are reactive by default, whether that's Angular's RxJS streams or React state that assumes data changes out from under it.

Performance work is concrete for me, not aspirational: cutting Letstream's dashboard load time by 40% came from auditing what actually blocked rendering and fixing that specifically, not from running a generic optimization checklist.

services.title: Backend & API Design
services.description: NestJS and Node.js services with explicit domain boundaries, API contracts and migration discipline.

paragraphs: An API is a promise to whoever calls it, so I design contracts to be explicit and hard to misuse — clear domain boundaries, predictable error shapes, and versioning discipline when something has to change.

I carry that same discipline through migrations: moving a team from one framework to another, or a dataset through a hierarchical resolution pipeline, works the same way — resolve ambiguity early, verify independently, and never let a "probably fine" assumption reach production.

services.title: Software Architecture
services.description: Event-driven and distributed system design, the focus of my M.Sc. studies.

paragraphs: This is the part of engineering I'm actively deepening through my M.Sc. — how systems stay correct and observable as they grow distributed, not just how to draw the diagram.

SynthGraph's lineage graph is where that's most concrete in my own work: tracking generation, training and evaluation as one connected system instead of isolated scripts, so a result can be traced back to exactly what produced it.

services.title: AI-assisted Engineering
services.description: Agentic coding workflows guided by explicit architecture and engineering guardrails.

paragraphs: I use agentic coding tools as engineers, not oracles, which means the guardrails matter more than the autonomy. Explicit architecture docs, a stability contract and a regression checklist turn an agent from something that moves fast and breaks things into something that moves fast inside boundaries I've actually reviewed.
This portfolio is itself built that way: every change an agent makes here goes through the same required-reading and verification process a human contributor would.
